verses.31:37: and if I did not tear it up and return it, taking nothing from the debtor—
verses.31:38: if the land has ever groaned against me, or if its furrows also have wept with one accord;
verses.31:39: or if I also ate its strength alone without price, or if I also took the life of the owner of the land and grieved him—
verses.31:40: then instead of wheat may nettles come forth for me, and instead of barley, brambles. And Job ceased from his words.
verses.32:1: Now his three friends also ceased answering Job further, for Job was righteous before them.
verses.32:2: Then Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the family of Ram, of the land of Ausitis, became angry; he was exceedingly angry with Job, because he declared himself righteous before the Lord.
verses.32:3: Against the three friends also he was exceedingly angry, because they were unable to answer Job in rebuttal, and yet they declared him to be ungodly.
verses.32:4: Now Elihu had waited to give an answer to Job, because they were older than he in days.
verses.32:5: And Elihu saw that there was no answer in the mouth of the three men, and he was provoked in his wrath.
verses.32:6: Then Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said, "I am younger in years, and you are older; therefore I kept silent, fearing to declare to you my own knowledge.
verses.32:7: And I said, 'It is not time that speaks, and in many years they do not know wisdom;
verses.32:8: rather, there is a spirit in mortals, and the breath of the Almighty is what teaches;
verses.32:9: it is not the long-lived who are wise, nor do the aged know judgment.'
verses.32:10: Therefore I said, 'Hear me, and I will declare to you what I know.'
verses.32:11: Give ear to my words while you listen, until you search out words.
verses.32:12: And I will give full attention to you; and behold, there was no one among you who refuted Job, or answered back his words.
verses.32:13: So that you may not say, 'We have found wisdom by joining ourselves to the Lord;'
verses.32:14: yet you permitted a man to speak such words.
verses.32:15: They were dismayed, they answered no more; they let words grow old from them.
verses.32:16: I waited, for I did not speak; because they stood still and did not answer."
verses.32:18: "Again I will speak; for I am full of words, for the spirit of my belly destroys me;
verses.32:19: and my belly is like a bound wineskin of fermenting new wine, or like a smith's bellows that has burst.
verses.32:20: I will speak, that I may find relief, opening my lips;
verses.32:21: for I will by no means be ashamed before a man, nor indeed will I stand in awe of a mortal;
verses.32:22: for I do not know how to show partiality to persons; otherwise, moths also will eat me."
verses.33:1: "Nevertheless, hear my words, O Job, and give ear to my speech;
verses.33:2: for behold, I have opened my mouth, and my tongue has spoken.
verses.33:3: My heart is pure in words, and the understanding of my lips shall conceive pure things.
verses.33:4: The divine Spirit is what made me, and the breath of the Almighty is what teaches me.
verses.33:5: If you are able, give me an answer to these things; stand firm, take your place facing me, and I facing you.
verses.33:6: Out of clay you have been formed, even as I also; out of the same we have been formed.
verses.33:7: Dread of me shall not terrify you, nor shall my hand be heavy upon you.
verses.33:8: Yet you have spoken in my ears, and I have heard the sound of words;
verses.33:9: because you say, 'I am pure, not having sinned; I am blameless, for I have not committed iniquity.
verses.33:10: Yet He has found fault against me, and He has regarded me as an adversary;
verses.33:11: He has put my foot in the stocks, and He has watched all my ways.'
verses.33:12: For how do you say, 'I am righteous, and He has not listened to me'? For He who is above mortals is eternal.
verses.33:13: And you say, 'Why has He not listened to every word of my cause?'
verses.33:14: For the Lord speaks once, and a second time:
verses.33:15: in a dream, or in a nightly meditation, as when a dreadful fear falls upon men, during slumberings upon a bed;
verses.33:16: then He uncovers the mind of men; with such visions of dread He terrifies them,
verses.33:17: to turn a man away from unrighteousness; and He delivers his body from a fall.
verses.33:18: And He spares his soul from death, and from falling in war.
verses.33:19: Again He chastens him with sickness upon his bed, and the multitude of his bones grows numb;
verses.33:20: and he is by no means able to receive any food of grain, though his soul will crave food;
verses.33:21: until his flesh rots away, and he displays his bones empty.
verses.33:22: And his soul draws near to death, and this life of his is in Hades;
verses.33:23: if there are a thousand death-bearing angels, not one of them shall wound him. If he determines in his heart to turn back to the Lord, and declares to man his own fault, and shows his folly,
verses.33:24: He will uphold him so that he does not fall into death; and He will renew his body like plaster upon a wall, and He will fill his bones with marrow;
verses.33:25: and He will make his flesh tender like that of a babe, and He will restore him grown to manhood among men.
verses.33:26: And when he has prayed to the Lord, his prayer shall be acceptable to Him, and he shall enter with a cheerful countenance with open confession; and He will render righteousness to men.
verses.33:27: Then at that time a man shall reproach himself, saying, 'What manner of things was I doing? And He has not chastened me according to what my sins deserved.
verses.33:28: Save my soul from going into corruption, and my life shall see the light.'
verses.33:29: Behold, the Mighty One works all these things in three ways with a man;
verses.33:30: yet He has delivered my soul from death, that my life may praise Him in the light.
verses.33:31: Give ear, O Job, and listen to me; keep silent, and I myself will speak.
verses.33:32: If there is a word, answer me; speak, for I desire that you be justified.
verses.33:33: If not, you listen to me; keep silent, and I will teach you."
verses.34:2: "Hear me, you wise men; you who have knowledge, give ear;
verses.34:3: for the ear tests words, and the palate tastes food.
verses.34:4: Let us choose judgment for ourselves; let us know among ourselves what is good.
verses.34:5: For Job has said, 'I am righteous; the Lord has removed my judgment,
verses.34:6: and He has dealt falsely with my judgment; violent is my arrow without injustice.'
verses.34:7: What man is like Job, drinking scorn like water,
verses.34:8: having not sinned nor acted ungodly, or shared a way with those who practice lawlessness, to walk with the ungodly?
verses.34:9: For do not say, 'There shall be no visitation for a man,' yet there is a visitation for him from the Lord.
verses.34:10: Therefore, you of understanding heart, hear me: Far be it from me to act ungodly before the Lord, and before the Almighty to confound justice;
verses.34:11: rather, He renders to a man according to what each of them does, and in the path of a man He shall find him.
verses.34:12: Now do you suppose that the Lord will do wrong? Or will the Almighty confound judgment,
verses.34:13: He who made the earth? And who is He who makes the world under heaven and all things that are in it?
verses.34:14: For if He should choose to hold back, and to retain the spirit with Himself,
verses.34:15: all flesh shall perish together, and every mortal shall depart to the earth from which he was also formed.
verses.34:16: Now if you are not admonished, hear these things; give ear to the voice of words.
verses.34:17: Behold Him who hates lawless deeds and destroys the wicked, who is eternally righteous.
verses.34:18: Ungodly is he who says to a king, 'You act lawlessly,' and to rulers, 'Most ungodly one!'—
verses.34:19: who does not feel shame before the face of an honorable man, nor knows how to bestow honor upon the great, so that their persons might be respected.
verses.34:20: And in vain shall it turn out for them to cry out and to implore a man; for they dealt lawlessly when the powerless were turned aside.
verses.34:21: For He Himself is the beholder of the works of men, and nothing of what they do is hidden from Him;
verses.34:22: nor shall there be any place for those who do lawless deeds to hide themselves;
verses.34:23: for He will no longer lay anything upon a man.
verses.34:24: For the Lord looks upon all—He who comprehends unsearchable things, both glorious and wondrous things, of which there is no number;
verses.34:25: He who knows their works; and He shall overturn the night, and it shall be brought low.
verses.34:26: And He has extinguished the ungodly, and they are visible before Him;
verses.34:27: because they turned aside from the law of God, and they did not acknowledge His ordinances,
verses.34:28: so as to bring upon Him the cry of the needy, and He shall hear the cry of the poor.
verses.34:29: And He Himself shall grant quietness, and who shall condemn? And He shall hide His face, and who shall behold Him—both against a nation and against a man alike,
verses.34:30: making a hypocritical man king because of the perversity of the people.
verses.34:31: For there is one who says to the Mighty One, 'I have received; I will not take a pledge;
verses.34:32: apart from myself I shall see; You show me; if I have wrought iniquity, I will surely do so no more.'
verses.34:33: Will He repay it from you, because you will reject it? For you shall choose, and not I; therefore speak what you know.
verses.34:34: Therefore those of understanding heart shall say these things, and a wise man has heard my word.
verses.34:35: But Job has not spoken with understanding; his words are not with knowledge.
verses.34:36: Nevertheless, learn, O Job: do not give an answer any longer like the foolish,
verses.34:37: lest we add to our sins, and lawlessness be reckoned against us while we speak many words before the Lord."
verses.35:2: "Why have you considered this in judgment? Who are you that you have said, 'I am righteous before the Lord'?
verses.35:4: I will give an answer to you, and to your three friends.
verses.35:5: Look up to heaven and see, and observe the clouds, how high they are above you.
verses.35:6: If you have sinned, what will you accomplish? And even if you have committed much lawlessness, what are you able to do?
verses.35:7: And since then you are righteous, what will you give to Him? Or what shall He receive from your hand?
verses.35:8: Your ungodliness is for a man like yourself, and your righteousness is for a son of man.
verses.35:9: Because of the multitude, those who are oppressed shall cry out; they shall shout aloud because of the arm of the many.
verses.35:10: Yet none has said, 'Where is God who made me, who appoints the night watches,
verses.35:11: who separates me from the four-footed beasts of the earth, and from the birds of heaven?'
verses.35:12: There they shall cry out, and He will by no means hear, even because of the arrogance of the wicked.
verses.35:13: For the Lord does not desire to look upon what is wrong; for He Himself, the Almighty, is the beholder
verses.35:14: of those who carry out lawless deeds, and He shall save me. Now be judged before Him, if you are able to praise Him as He is.
verses.35:15: And now, because He is not visiting His wrath, and has not greatly taken note of any transgression,
verses.35:16: Job opens his mouth in vain; in ignorance he makes words heavy."
verses.36:1: And Elihu continued further and said:
verses.36:2: "Wait for me a little longer, that I may teach you; for there is still speech within me.
verses.36:3: Taking up my knowledge from afar, in my works I will speak righteous things in truth,
verses.36:4: and not unrighteous words; you understand unrighteously.
verses.36:5: Yet know that the Lord will by no means reject the innocent; mighty in strength of heart,
verses.36:6: He will by no means keep the ungodly alive, and He will grant justice to the poor.
verses.36:7: He will not withdraw His eyes from the righteous, and with kings upon a throne He will seat them in victory, and they shall be exalted.
verses.36:8: And those who are bound in fetters shall be held fast in cords of poverty;
verses.36:9: and He will declare to them their works and their transgressions, because they will grow strong.
verses.36:10: But He will heed the righteous; and He said that they shall turn back from unrighteousness.
verses.36:11: If they hear and serve, they shall complete their days in good things, and their years in splendor.
verses.36:12: But the ungodly He does not preserve, because they were unwilling to know the Lord, and because, when admonished, they were disobedient.
verses.36:13: And the hypocrites in heart shall marshal wrath; they shall not cry out because He has bound them.
verses.36:14: Therefore let their soul die in youth, and their life be wounded by angels,
verses.36:15: because they afflicted the weak and the powerless; yet He will set forth the judgment of the meek.
verses.36:16: And an abyss has further deceived you from the mouth of an enemy, an outpouring beneath it, and your table went down full of fatness.
verses.36:17: Yet justice shall not be lacking from the righteous,
verses.36:18: but wrath shall be upon the ungodly, because of the ungodliness of the gifts which they received for unrighteous deeds.
verses.36:19: Do not let your mind willingly turn you aside from the supplication of the powerless who are in distress,
verses.36:20: and all those who exert strength. Do not draw out the night, for peoples to go up in their place;
verses.36:21: but take heed that you do not practice unrighteous things; for on this account you have chosen out of poverty.
verses.36:22: Behold, the Mighty One shall act mightily in His strength; for who is a sovereign like Him?
verses.36:23: And who is he who examines His works? Or who is he who has said, 'He has done unrighteous things'?
verses.36:24: Remember that His works are great, over which men have ruled;
verses.36:25: every man has seen within himself, as many mortals as are wounded.
verses.36:26: Behold, the Mighty One is great, and we shall not know Him; the number of His years is indeed boundless.
verses.36:27: And the drops of rain are numbered by Him, and they shall be poured out in rain into a cloud;
verses.36:28: The ancient things shall flow, and the clouds have cast a shadow over countless mortals. He has appointed a season for the beasts, and they know the order of their resting place. At all these things is your mind not astounded, nor is your heart parted from your body?
verses.36:29: And if anyone understands the outspreadings of a cloud, the evenness of His tabernacle,
verses.36:30: behold, the song shall stretch out upon Him, and He has covered the roots of the sea.
verses.36:31: For by these He shall judge peoples; He shall give food to the one who hears.
verses.36:32: Upon His hands He has covered the light, and He has given command concerning it against the one who meets it;
verses.36:33: He will declare His friend concerning Him: the Lord is a possession, even concerning unrighteousness."
verses.37:1: "At this also my heart has been troubled, and has slipped away from its place.
verses.37:2: Hear a sound in the wrath of the Lord's anger, and a meditation shall go forth from His mouth.
verses.37:3: Beneath all heaven is His dominion, and His light is upon the wings of the earth.
verses.37:4: After it He shall cry out with a voice; He shall thunder with the voice of His pride, and He shall not exchange them, for you shall hear His voice.
verses.37:5: The Mighty One shall thunder wondrous things with His voice, for He has done great things which we did not know;
verses.37:6: commanding the snow, 'Be upon the earth,' and the storm of rain, and the storm of the rains of His might.
verses.37:7: He sets a seal upon the hand of every man, that every man may know his own weakness.
verses.37:8: And the wild beasts entered under shelter, and grew quiet in their lair.
verses.37:9: Out of the chambers come pains, and from the promontories comes cold.
verses.37:10: And from the breath of the Mighty One He shall give frost, and He steers the water however He wills;
verses.37:11: and a cloud spreads over what is choice. A cloud shall scatter His light.
verses.37:12: And He Himself shall turn about the circuits, in theebulathoth for their works; all things whatever He commands them, these have been ordained by Him upon the earth,
verses.37:13: whether for discipline, whether for His land, whether for mercy, He shall find him.
verses.37:14: Give ear to these things, Job; stand still, being instructed in the power of the Lord.
verses.37:15: We know that God has established His works, having made light out of darkness.
verses.37:16: And He knows the separation of the clouds, and the extraordinary downfalls of the wicked.
verses.37:17: And your robe is warm; and there is stillness upon the earth.
verses.37:18: You will make firm with Him for the ancient things, strong as the appearance of a molten casting.
verses.37:19: Why? Teach me what we shall say to Him; and let us cease speaking many things.
verses.37:20: Does a book or a scribe stand beside me, that standing up I should silence a man?
verses.37:21: Yet the light is not visible to all; it shines afar in the ancient things, just as that which is from Him upon the clouds.
verses.37:22: From the north come clouds shining like gold; upon these, great is the glory and honor of the Almighty.
verses.37:23: And we do not find another equal to His strength; He who judges righteous things, do you not suppose that He listens?
verses.37:24: Therefore men shall fear Him, and the wise in heart also shall fear Him."
verses.38:1: Now after Elihu ceased speaking, the Lord said to Job through a whirlwind and clouds:
verses.38:2: "Who is this who hides counsel from Me, and holds back words in his heart, and thinks to conceal them from Me?
verses.38:3: Gird your loins like a man; I will question you, and you answer Me.
verses.38:4: Where were you when I founded the earth? Declare to Me, if you know understanding.
verses.38:5: Who appointed its measures, if you know? Or who is it who laid a measuring line upon it?
verses.38:6: Upon what have its rings been fastened? And who is it who laid a cornerstone upon it?
verses.38:7: When the stars were made, all My angels praised Me with a loud voice.
verses.38:8: And I hedged the sea with gates when it surged furiously, coming forth from its mother's womb;
verses.38:9: and I made a cloud its garment, and swaddled it in mist;
verses.38:10: and I set boundaries for it, placing bars and gates around it;
verses.38:11: and I said to it, 'Thus far you shall come, and you shall not pass beyond, but within yourself your waves shall be shattered.'
verses.38:12: Or was it in your days that I commanded the morning light, and the morning star beheld its own appointed station,
verses.38:13: to take hold of the wings of the earth, to shake the ungodly out of it?
verses.38:14: Or did you take clay of the earth and fashion a living creature, and set him upon the earth able to speak?
verses.38:15: And have you taken away the light from the ungodly, and shattered the arm of the proud?
verses.38:16: And have you come to the spring of the sea, and walked in the tracks of the abyss?
verses.38:17: Do the gates of death open to you in fear, and did the gatekeepers of Hades cower when they saw you?
verses.38:18: Have you perceived the breadth of what lies under heaven? Declare now to Me how vast it is.
verses.38:19: In what land does light dwell, and what is the place of darkness?
verses.38:20: Could you lead Me to their borders? And do you also know their paths?
verses.38:21: I know, then, that you were born at that time, and the number of your years is great.
verses.38:22: Have you come to the treasuries of snow, and have you seen the treasuries of hail?
verses.38:23: Are they laid up for you against an hour of enemies, for a day of wars and battle?
verses.38:24: From where does the frost come forth, or the south wind scatter abroad over what lies under heaven?
verses.38:25: And who has prepared a course for the torrential rain, and a way for the tumults,
verses.38:26: to bring rain upon a land where there is no man, a wilderness in which no mortal dwells,
verses.38:27: to satisfy the untrodden and uninhabited waste, and to cause the sprouting of tender grass?
verses.38:28: Who is the father of the rain? And who is it who has given birth to the drops of dew?
verses.38:29: From whose womb does the ice come forth? And who has given birth to the frost in heaven,
verses.38:30: which descends like flowing water? And who has terrified the face of the ungodly?
verses.38:31: Do you understand the bond of the Pleiades, and have you opened the enclosure of Orion?
verses.38:32: Or will you open Mazoroth in its season, and the Evening Star by its locks—will you lead them?
verses.38:33: Do you know the turnings of heaven, or all the things that come to pass in unison under heaven?
verses.38:34: Will you call a cloud with your voice, and with a violent trembling of water will it obey you?
verses.38:35: Will you send forth thunderbolts, and will they go? And will they say to you, 'What is it?'
verses.38:36: And who gave to women the wisdom of weaving, or the knowledge of embroidery?
verses.38:37: And who is it who numbers the clouds in wisdom, and has bowed heaven down to the earth?
verses.38:38: Dust is poured out like earth, and I have bonded it as a cube to a stone.
verses.38:39: Will you hunt prey for the lions, and fill the souls of the dragons?
verses.38:40: For they shrink in fear in their dens, and sit in the thickets lying in ambush.
verses.38:41: And who has prepared food for the raven? For its young have cried out to the Lord, wandering about seeking their food."
verses.39:1: "Do you know the time of birth of the wild mountain goats of the rock, and have you watched over the birth pangs of the deer?
verses.39:2: Have you numbered their full months until birth, and have you loosed their birth pangs?
verses.39:3: Have you reared their young ones free from fear? Will you send away their birth pangs?
verses.39:4: Their offspring will break away, they will multiply in increase; they will go forth, and will by no means return to them.
verses.39:5: And who is it who has set the wild donkey free, and who has loosed his bonds?
verses.39:6: I have appointed the wilderness as his habitation, and the salt land as his dwellings.
verses.39:7: Laughing at the thronging multitude of the city, and not hearing the rebuke of the tax collector,
verses.39:8: he will survey the mountains, his pasture, and he searches after every green thing.
verses.39:9: Will the unicorn be willing to serve you, or to lie down by your manger?
verses.39:10: Will you bind his yoke with straps, or will he draw your furrows in the plain?
verses.39:11: Do you trust in him because his strength is great, and will you leave your labors to him?
verses.39:12: Will you trust that he will return the seed to you, and bring in your threshing floor?
verses.39:13: The wing of those who delight—if the hasida and the nessa should conceive;
verses.39:14: for she will leave her eggs in the earth, and warm them upon the dust;
verses.39:15: and they have forgotten that a foot will scatter them, and the wild beasts of the field will trample them.
verses.39:16: She has dealt harshly with her own young, as though they were not her own; in vain she has labored without fear.
verses.39:17: For God has kept wisdom silent from her, and has not given her a share in understanding.
verses.39:18: In her season she will lift herself up on high; she will laugh at the horse and his rider.
verses.39:19: Or have you invested the horse with strength, and clothed his neck with terror?
verses.39:20: Have you clothed him with full armor, and the glory of his breast with boldness?
verses.39:21: Pawing in the plain, he exults, and goes forth into the plain in strength;
verses.39:22: meeting a king, he laughs, and will by no means turn back from iron.
verses.39:23: Upon him the bow and the sword exult,
verses.39:24: and in wrath he will make the earth vanish; and he will by no means believe until a trumpet sounds.
verses.39:25: When the trumpet sounds, he says, 'Aha!' And from afar he catches the scent of war, with leaping and shouting.
verses.39:26: Is it by your knowledge that the hawk stands poised, spreading out its wings motionless, gazing toward the south?
verses.39:27: And at your command does the eagle soar on high, and does the vulture, settling upon its nest, abide
verses.39:28: upon a crag of the rock and in a hidden place?
verses.39:29: Being there, it seeks its food; from afar its eyes keep watch;
verses.39:30: and its young wallow in blood, and wherever the dead are, immediately they are found."
verses.40:1: And the Lord God answered Job and said,
verses.40:2: "Will anyone turn aside judgment with the Sufficient One? And he who reproves God, shall he answer it?"
verses.40:3: Then Job answered and said to the Lord,
verses.40:4: "Why am I still judged, being admonished and reproving the Lord, hearing such things though I am nothing? And what answer shall I give to these things? I will lay my hand upon my mouth.
verses.40:5: Once I have spoken, but a second time I will not continue."
verses.40:6: Then the Lord answered Job again out of the cloud and said,
verses.40:7: "No, rather gird up your loins like a man; I will question you, and you answer Me.
verses.40:8: Do not cast aside My judgment. Do you think that I have dealt with you in any other way than that you might be shown righteous?
verses.40:9: Or do you have an arm against the Lord, or do you thunder with a voice against Him?
verses.40:10: Take up now loftiness and power, and clothe yourself with glory and honor.
verses.40:11: Send forth angels in wrath, and humble every insolent one,
verses.40:12: and extinguish the proud; cause the ungodly to decay at once,
verses.40:13: and hide them in the earth together, and fill their faces with dishonor.
verses.40:14: Then I will confess that your right hand is able to save.
verses.40:15: Yet now, behold wild beasts beside you; they eat grass like oxen.
verses.40:16: Behold now, his strength is in his loins, and his power is in the navel of his belly.
verses.40:17: He sets up his tail like a cypress, and his sinews are intertwined.
verses.40:18: His ribs are ribs of bronze, and his backbone is cast iron.
verses.40:19: This is the beginning of the Lord's creation, made to be mocked by His angels.
verses.40:20: And going up upon a steep mountain, he brings joy to the four-footed beasts in Tartarus.
verses.40:21: He lies down beneath trees of every kind, beside the papyrus and reed and sedge.
verses.40:22: And great trees cast shade over him with their shoots, and the branches of the field.
verses.40:23: If a flood arises, he will by no means notice it; he is confident that the Jordan will dash against his mouth.
verses.40:24: Will anyone take him before his eye? Acting craftily, will one pierce his nose?
verses.40:25: And will you draw a dragon with a hook, and put a halter around his nose?
verses.40:26: Will you bind a ring in his nostril, and pierce his lip with a clasp?
verses.40:27: Will he speak to you with supplication, softly with petition?
verses.40:28: Will he make a covenant with you? And will you take him as a perpetual servant?
verses.40:29: Will you play with him as with a bird, or bind him like a sparrow for a child?
verses.40:30: Do the nations feed upon him, and do the nations of the Phoenicians divide him up?
verses.40:31: Every sailing vessel gathered together could by no means carry one hide of his tail, nor his head in the boats of fishermen.
verses.40:32: And you will lay a hand upon him, remembering the battle that takes place in his body."
verses.41:1: "Have you not even marveled at the things spoken? And do you not fear that he is prepared for Me?
verses.41:2: Do you not fear that he is prepared for Me? For who is he who has withstood Me?
verses.41:3: For who is he who has withstood Me? Or who will withstand Me and endure? If all that is under heaven is Mine,
verses.41:4: I will not be silent because of him, and as for a word of power, he will pity his equal.
verses.41:5: Who will uncover the face of his garment? And who could enter into the fold of his breastplate?
verses.41:6: Who will open the gates of his face? Around his teeth is terror.
verses.41:7: His inward parts are shields of bronze, and his bond is like an emery stone.
verses.41:8: One is joined fast to another, and wind shall by no means pass through him.
verses.41:9: Each shall cleave to his brother; they hold fast together and shall by no means be torn apart.
verses.41:10: In his sneezing a radiance shines forth, and his eyes are the appearance of the morning star.
verses.41:11: Out of his mouth go forth burning torches, and braziers of fire are hurled abroad.
verses.41:12: Out of his nostrils goes forth the smoke of a furnace burning with a fire of coals.
verses.41:13: His breath is coals, and a flame goes forth out of his mouth.
verses.41:14: In his neck strength abides, and destruction runs before him.
verses.41:15: The flesh of his body is joined fast together; one pours down upon him, yet he shall not be shaken.
verses.41:16: His heart is hardened like a stone, and stands firm like an unyielding anvil.
verses.41:17: And when he turns, terror comes upon the four-footed beasts leaping upon the earth.
verses.41:18: If spears meet him, they shall accomplish nothing—neither lance nor breastplate.
verses.41:19: For he regards iron as chaff, and bronze as rotten wood.
verses.41:20: A bow of bronze shall by no means wound him; he counts a stone-thrower as grass,
verses.41:21: hammers are reckoned as stubble, and he laughs at the shaking of a firebrand.
verses.41:22: His bed is sharp spikes, and all the gold of the sea beneath him is like untold mire.
verses.41:23: He makes the abyss boil like a cauldron; he regards the sea as an ointment pot,
verses.41:24: and the Tartarus of the abyss as a captive; he has reckoned the abyss as a walkway.
verses.41:25: There is nothing upon the earth like him, made to be mocked by My angels.
verses.41:26: He beholds every lofty thing, and he is king over all things in the waters."
verses.42:1: Then Job responded and said to the Lord:
verses.42:2: "I know that You are able to do all things, and nothing is impossible with You.
verses.42:3: For who is he who hides counsel from You? And sparing words, does he think to hide from You also? And who will declare to me the things I did not know, things great and marvelous which I did not understand?
verses.42:4: Now hear me, O Lord, that I also may speak; I will ask, and You teach me.
verses.42:5: By the hearing of the ear I heard of You before, but now my eye has seen You.
verses.42:6: Therefore I have despised myself and melted away, and I regard myself as earth and ashes."
verses.42:7: Now it came to pass, after the Lord had spoken all these words to Job, that the Lord said to Eliphaz the Temanite, "You have sinned, you and your friends; for you have not spoken anything true before Me, as My servant Job has.
verses.42:8: Now therefore, take seven calves and seven rams, and go to My servant Job, and he shall offer burnt offerings for you. And My servant Job shall pray for you, for only his person will I accept; for were it not for his sake, I would have destroyed you, because you have not spoken what is true concerning My servant Job."
verses.42:9: So Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Minaean went and did as the Lord had commanded them; and He remitted their sin on account of Job.
verses.42:10: And the Lord increased Job; and when he prayed for his friends as well, He forgave them their sin; and the Lord gave Job double of all that he had before, in twofold measure.
verses.42:11: Then all his brothers and his sisters heard all the things that had happened to him, and came to him, together with all who had known him from the first; and they ate and drank with him, and comforted him, and marveled at all that the Lord had brought upon him; and each one gave him one ewe lamb and a tetradrachm of uncoined gold.
verses.42:12: And the Lord blessed the latter days of Job more than the former; and his livestock was fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, one thousand yoke of oxen, and one thousand grazing female donkeys.
verses.42:13: And seven sons and three daughters were born to him.
verses.42:14: And he called the first Day, the second Cassia, and the third Horn of Amalthea.
verses.42:15: And none were found like the daughters of Job, nor better than they, in the earth under heaven; and their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers.
verses.42:16: And Job lived after his affliction one hundred and seventy years, and all the years that he lived were two hundred and forty; and Job saw his sons and his sons' sons, to the fourth generation.
verses.42:17: And Job died, old and full of days. And it is written that he will rise again with those whom the Lord raises up. This man is interpreted from the Syriac book as dwelling in the land of Ausitis, on the borders of Idumea and Arabia; and his former name was Jobab. And taking an Arabian wife, he fathered a son whose name was Ennon; and he himself was of his father Zerah, a son of the sons of Esau, and of his mother Bozrah, so that he was the fifth from Abraham. And these are the kings who reigned in Edom, over which land he also ruled: first, Balak the son of Beor, and the name of his city was Dinhabah; and after Balak, Jobab, who is called Job; and after him, Husham, who was governor from the Temanite land; and after him, Hadad the son of Barad, who cut down Midian in the plain of Moab, and the name of his city was Geththaim. And the friends who came to him were Eliphaz, of the sons of Esau, king of the Temanites; Bildad, sovereign of the Shuhites; and Zophar, king of the Minaeans.

notes.1:1: "Ausitis" preserves the Septuagint regional name (Αὐσῖτις), corresponding to Uz in the Hebrew text.
notes.1:5: The Septuagint uniquely specifies "one calf for a sin offering for their souls" alongside the sacrifices Job offered for his children.
notes.1:6: The Greek reads "the angels of God" (οἱ ἄγγελοι τοῦ θεοῦ) and "the devil" (ὁ διάβολος, lit. "the slanderer"), corresponding to "the sons of God" and "the adversary" (Satan) in the Hebrew text.
notes.1:11: The Greek verb εὐλογήσει ("will bless") preserves the ancient scribal euphemism for cursing God (also in 2:5).
notes.2:8: The Septuagint specifies that Job sat "upon the dunghill outside the city" and uses ἰχώρ ("discharge") for the fluid scraped from his sores.
notes.2:9: The Septuagint includes a substantial expansion of Job's wife's lament, recounting her grief over their lost children and her wandering as a hired servant before urging Job to speak against the Lord and die.
notes.2:11: The Septuagint assigns royal titles ("king," "ruler," "king") to Job's three friends and identifies Zophar as king of the "Minaeans" (Μειναίων), where the Hebrew text reads "the Naamathite."
notes.3:8: "The great sea monster" translates τὸ μέγα κῆτος, the Septuagint rendering corresponding to Leviathan in the Hebrew text.
notes.3:14: The Septuagint reads "who prided themselves upon swords" (ἐπὶ ξίφεσιν), reflecting a reading of the Hebrew consonants as "sword" rather than "ruins."
notes.3:18: "The eternal ones" (οἱ αἰώνιοι) designates the dead in the eternal abode, where the Hebrew text reads "the prisoners"; similarly, "tax collector" (φορολόγου) corresponds to "taskmaster."
notes.3:23: The Septuagint opens the verse with "Death is rest for a man," whereas the Hebrew text reads "to a man whose way is hidden."
notes.4:6: The Greek reads 'in folly' and 'the wickedness of your way,' turning Eliphaz's question into a direct reproach of Job's piety and conduct, in contrast to the Hebrew Masoretic Text's reference to 'your confidence' and 'the integrity of your ways.'
notes.4:10: The Greek speaks of the exultation of 'dragons' (drakontōn) rather than the teeth of young lions found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.4:11: The Greek renders the rare poetic term for a lion with myrmēkoleōn ('ant-lion'), a composite creature known in ancient natural lore.
notes.4:16: The Greek uses the first-person verb 'I arose' (anestēn) describing Eliphaz's reaction, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text describes the apparition standing still; the voice's quotation in 4:17 closes before Eliphaz speaks in the first-person plural ('we ourselves') in 4:19.
notes.5:4: The rare Greek verb kolabrizō denotes treating with mocking contempt or humiliation, and the Greek specifies 'the doors of inferiors' rather than the city gate of the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.5:5: The rare Greek verb eksiphōnizō literally means to draw out with a siphon, vividly picturing the strength or wealth of the wicked being drained dry.
notes.5:7: The Greek renders the poetic Hebrew phrase for sparks or winged flames as 'the young of the vulture' (neossoi gypos) flying in the heights.
notes.5:23: The Greek omits the clause concerning a covenant with the stones of the field present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, preserving a concise statement of peace with wild beasts.
notes.6:4: The Greek reads "my blood" and "whenever I begin to speak, they pierce me," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "my spirit" and speaks of the terrors of God arrayed against Job.
notes.6:6: The Greek reads "in empty words," a notable Septuagint rendering where the Hebrew Masoretic Text refers to the taste of purslane juice or egg white.
notes.6:7: Greek bromon (a variant spelling of bromos, "stench") parallels "the smell of a lion," expressing Job's revulsion at his food.
notes.6:9: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text, in which Job asks God to cut him off completely, the Greek includes the negative particle me ("not"): "yet let Him not utterly destroy me."
notes.6:19: Greek Thaimanon refers to the "Temanites" (rather than the caravans of Tema as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text), echoing Eliphaz the Temanite.
notes.7:5: The Greek depicts Job dissolving clods of earth while scraping away watery discharge (ichor) from his sores.
notes.7:6: The Greek reads "swifter than speech" (lalias), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "swifter than a weaver's shuttle."
notes.7:15: Whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text expresses Job's preference for strangling and death over his bones, the Greek addresses God directly: "You will separate my soul from my spirit, and my bones from death."
notes.7:18: The Greek renders the Hebrew idiom for "every moment" as eis anapausin ("until rest"), connecting the Hebrew root with resting.
notes.7:20: Greek katenteukten means "accuser" or "opponent" (rather than "target"), and "a burden upon You" preserves a well-known Septuagint reading where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "a burden to myself."
notes.8:12: Follows the Greek wording 'before drinking' (pro tou piein) and 'every herb' (pasa botane), differing from the Masoretic Hebrew 'before any other grass'.
notes.8:16: The Greek reads 'out of his decay' (ek saprias autou), contrasting with the Masoretic Hebrew 'over his garden'.
notes.8:18: The Greek verb katapie ('swallows up') has no explicit object, and the final clause ('you have not seen such things') is second-person singular rather than a first-person denial by the place as in the Hebrew.
notes.9:5: The Greek reads 'wears away' or 'makes old' (palaion) rather than the Masoretic Hebrew 'removes'.
notes.9:9: The Greek names Hesperus (the Evening Star) alongside the Pleiades and Arcturus, whereas the Hebrew lists the Bear, Orion, and the Pleiades.
notes.9:13: Unlike the Masoretic Hebrew ('God will not turn back His anger'), the Greek lacks a negative particle ('He Himself has turned aside wrath') and renders the Hebrew 'helpers of Rahab' as 'the sea monsters beneath heaven'.
notes.9:22: The Greek reads 'Wrath destroys the great and the mighty', differing from the Masoretic Hebrew ('He destroys the blameless and the wicked').
notes.9:24: The Greek opens with a plural verb referring to the righteous of verse 23 ('they have been delivered'), yet retains the feminine singular pronoun 'its' (autes, reflecting 'the earth') in 'its judges'.
notes.10:2: The Greek reads "Do not teach me to be ungodly" (me me asebein didaske), differing from the Hebrew "Do not condemn me."
notes.10:3: In the Greek text, Job is the subject of the first two verbs ("if I do wrong, that I should renounce the works of Your hands"), whereas the Hebrew makes God the subject.
notes.10:16: The Greek uses the passive "I am hunted like a lion for slaughter," portraying Job as the prey rather than comparing God to a hunting lion as in the Hebrew.
notes.11:1: The Greek identifies Zophar as "the Minaean" (ho Meinaios), a distinct Septuagint gentilic compared to "the Naamathite" of the Hebrew text.
notes.11:3: The opening line "Blessed is the short-lived man born of woman" is distinctive to the Greek text, replacing the Hebrew rhetorical question about idle talk.
notes.11:6: The Greek states that what has befallen Job from the Lord is "worthy of the sins you have committed," contrasting with the Hebrew statement that God exacts less than Job's iniquity deserves.
notes.12:3: The Greek preserves a briefer form of this verse, omitting the parallel clauses found in the Hebrew regarding not being inferior to the friends.
notes.12:11: The Greek reads "the mind" (nous) discerns words rather than "the ear" of the Hebrew text.
notes.12:18: The Greek reads "He seats kings upon thrones" rather than "He loosens the bond of kings" of the Hebrew text.
notes.12:21: The Greek concludes "and heals the lowly" (tapeinous de iasato), differing from the Hebrew "and loosens the belt of the strong."
notes.13:3: The Greek text reads "if He wills" (ἐὰν βούληται), diverging from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "I desire [to argue with God]."
notes.13:15: The Septuagint differs markedly from the well-known Hebrew reading ("Though He slay me, yet will I hope in Him"), stating instead that even if the Mighty One overpowers Job as He has already begun to do, Job will still speak and reason before Him.
notes.13:22: In the Greek text, God is the speaker in both clauses ("You will call... or You will speak") and Job is the respondent, whereas in the Hebrew text Job proposes speaking first in the second clause.
notes.14:5: The Greek text shifts abruptly from the third-person pronoun ("by Him," παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ) to the second-person verb ("You have set," ἔθου), a shift preserved literally in the translation.
notes.14:12: The unusual Greek phrase "until the heaven is no longer sewn together" (ἕως ἂν ὁ οὐρανὸς οὐ μὴ συνραφῇ) employs a double negative to depict the permanence of death while the heavens hold together.
notes.14:14: Unlike the Hebrew rhetorical question ("If a man dies, shall he live again?"), the Greek text as punctuated here presents an affirmative statement of life after death ("For if a man dies, he shall live... until I come into being again").
notes.15:2: The Greek reads "windy understanding" and "pain of the belly," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text speaks of "windy knowledge" and filling the belly with the "east wind."
notes.15:11: The Septuagint reads "for little of what you have sinned have you been scourged," differing markedly from the Hebrew text's question concerning the "consolations of God."
notes.15:18: The Greek places "their fathers" in the accusative ("did not conceal their fathers"), rather than the Hebrew prepositional phrase "from their fathers."
notes.15:34: The Greek reads "testimony" (martyrion), reflecting a different vocalization of the Hebrew consonantal root rendered "company" in the Masoretic Text.
notes.16:6: The Septuagint literally reads "I shall not feel the pain of the wound" rather than the Hebrew "my pain is not assuaged," framing Job's dilemma in Greek as being wounded whether he speaks or remains silent.
notes.16:8: The Greek reads "my falsehood" (to pseudos mou), rendering a Hebrew root that can signify either "leanness" or "falsehood."
notes.16:15: The Septuagint uses the third-person plural ("They sewed sackcloth"), continuing the actions of Job's assailants, whereas the Hebrew has the first-person singular ("I have sewed").
notes.16:20: The Greek reads "May my supplication reach the Lord," diverging from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "My friends scorn me."
notes.17:3: The Septuagint diverges markedly from the Masoretic Text's plea for a pledge, reading instead that strangers have stolen Job's possessions and demanding that the offender be bound to his hand.
notes.17:5: The Greek reads "evils" rather than "friends," reflecting a different vocalization of the underlying Hebrew consonants, followed by the image of eyes wasting away over sons.
notes.17:11: "The joints of my heart" translates Greek arthra ("joints" or "sinews"), rendering the Hebrew imagery of broken heartstrings or desires.
notes.18:3: Greek sesiōpēkamen ("we have been silent") reflects a different reading of the underlying Hebrew verb, where the Masoretic Text speaks of being regarded as stupid or defiled.
notes.18:9: The Greek leaves the subject of "will strengthen" unstated (understood here as God) and translates the Hebrew term for a snare as dipsōntas ("the thirsty").
notes.18:13: "The branches of his feet" literally translates Greek klōnes podōn, rendering the Hebrew term for limbs as "branches" (referring to the extremities of his feet), while omitting "firstborn of" before "death."
notes.18:17: The Greek critical text lacks a negative particle before hyparchei ("belongs/exists"), literally stating that a name belongs to him "upon the face outside," in contrast to the Masoretic Text's "he has no name in the street."
notes.19:17: The Septuagint reads "sons of my concubines," whereas the Masoretic Text refers to the sons of Job's own body or mother's womb.
notes.19:20: In place of the Masoretic Text's "by the skin of my teeth," the Greek describes Job's flesh rotting within his skin and his bones being held in his teeth.
notes.19:25: The Septuagint distinctively describes Job's Vindicator as "eternal" (aenaos) and "He who is about to deliver me," followed in verse 26 by the optative prayer that He may raise up Job's enduring skin upon the earth.
notes.19:29: Greek epikalymma ("covering" or "concealment") and hylē ("material" or "substance") are distinctive Septuagint renderings where the Masoretic Text warns of the sword and judgment.
notes.20:1: The Septuagint identifies Zophar as "the Minaean" (Greek Meinaíos, associated with the Minaean people of Arabia), rather than the Masoretic "Naamathite."
notes.20:6: The Greek text reads "his gifts" and "his sacrifice," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text refers to the wicked man's height and his head.
notes.20:15: The Septuagint uniquely reads "an angel shall drag him out of his house" rather than God casting wealth out of the man's belly; the Greek pronoun "him" could alternatively refer to "wealth."
notes.20:29: "The Overseer" translates Greek ho epískopos, a distinctive Septuagint divine title emphasizing God's watchful governance.
notes.21:2: The Septuagint includes a negative particle ("so that this consolation may not be mine from you"), rejecting the friends' comfort, whereas the Masoretic Text invites their listening to serve as their consolation.
notes.21:13: The Greek reads "in the rest of Hades they have fallen asleep," depicting a peaceful end for the ungodly rather than the sudden descent to Sheol in the Masoretic Text.
notes.21:15: "The Sufficient One" translates Greek Hikanós, the Septuagint of Job's characteristic rendering of the Hebrew divine name Shaddai.
notes.21:22: The Septuagint reads "He Himself shall judge murders" (phónous), differing from the Masoretic Text's reference to judging those on high.
notes.22:3: The Greek reads aposes ('put away' or 'cast off'), whereas some Septuagint witnesses read haploses ('make plain' or 'straighten').
notes.22:15: The Septuagint reads 'righteous men' (andres dikaioi), contrasting with the Hebrew Masoretic Text ('wicked men').
notes.22:21: Greek skleros literally means 'hard' or 'firm,' rendered here as 'steadfast,' differing from the Hebrew sense of agreeing or reconciling with God.
notes.22:24: 'Sophir' (Sopheir) is the distinctive Septuagint Greek form of the place name Ophir.
notes.23:5: The Greek reads iamata ('remedies' or 'healings'), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ('words') and possibly reflecting an early Greek shift from rhemata ('words').
notes.23:8: The Greek has the first-person verb 'I am no more' (ouk eti eimi), rather than the third-person 'He is not there' of the Hebrew text.
notes.23:15: Verse 14 of the Hebrew numbering is absent from the Greek text, and verse 15 preserves a doubled rendering of Job's dismay before God.
notes.24:5: The Greek clause 'having gone out of their own order beyond me' (hyper emou exelthontes ten heauton taxin) is an obscure Septuagint rendering that diverges sharply from the Hebrew text.
notes.24:17: Greek tarachos is translated here as a Koine neuter accusative ('the terror'); if read as masculine nominative, the clause means 'for the terror of the shadow of death will recognize them.'
notes.24:21: Greek agynaion literally denotes an unmarried or wifeless person, used here where the Hebrew text refers to a widow.
notes.25:2: Greek "prooimion" ("prelude" or "opening") reflects reading the Hebrew root for "proverb/discourse" rather than "dominion," and "the whole universe" ("ten sympasan") appears where the Masoretic Text has "peace."
notes.25:3: The Septuagint reads "delay for raiders" and "an ambush from Him," differing notably from the Masoretic Text's "number to his armies" and "his light."
notes.25:6: Greek "ea de" is an emphatic interjection ("alas, then" or "let be"), rendering the Hebrew "how much less" expression.
notes.26:2: In verses 2-3, the Septuagint turns the questions into pointed irony, asking whether Bildad is rushing to aid and counsel One who already possesses great strength, all wisdom, and the greatest power.
notes.26:5: Greek "gigantes" ("giants") renders the Hebrew Rephaim (shades of the dead), and "maiothesontai" literally means "be brought to birth" or "delivered as by a midwife."
notes.26:10: Greek "prostagma" ("decree" or "ordinance") translates a Hebrew noun that can mean either "boundary" or "statute."
notes.26:13: The Septuagint reads "bars of heaven" ("kleithra ouranou") and "rebellious dragon" ("drakonta apostaten"), where the Masoretic Text has "the heavens were made fair" and "the fleeing serpent."
notes.27:6: Greek "ou gar synoida emauto atopa praxas" ("I am not conscious within myself of having done anything wrong") uses an idiom of conscience where the Masoretic Text speaks of Job's heart not reproaching any of his days.
notes.27:8: The Septuagint asks whether the ungodly man will be saved by trusting in the Lord, diverging from the Masoretic Text's reference to God cutting off and taking away his life.
notes.27:15: The Septuagint lacks the first half of the Masoretic verse ("those who survive him are buried by pestilence") and reads "no one shall have mercy on their widows" instead of "his widows do not weep."
notes.27:23: The Greek pairs singular future verbs ("krotesei" and "syriei") with the plural phrase "their hands" ("cheiras auton"), reflecting an impersonal or collective subject rendered here as "They."
notes.28:4: Greek apo konias ("away from limestone" or "from dust") reflects reading the Hebrew consonant group as "chalk/lime" rather than "sojourner," and the second clause ("those who forget the righteous way") is a distinctive Septuagint rendering.
notes.28:10: The Septuagint reads mou ho ophthalmos ("my eye") rather than the Hebrew "his eye," and in verse 11 heautou dynamin ("his own power") rather than "the hidden thing." The unnamed third-person subject in verses 3 and 9-11 refers in context to the miner, though some ancient Greek commentators understood it of God.
notes.28:15: Greek synkleismon ("enclosure") renders the Hebrew term for fine gold etymologically from the root meaning "to shut in."
notes.28:16: Sophir preserves the Septuagint proper name Sopheir (Hebrew "Ophir").
notes.28:18: The Septuagint renders Hebrew gem terms etymologically as "lofty things" (meteora) and "the innermost things" (ta esotata), leaves gabeis ("gabis," crystal) untranslated, and reads an imperative "draw up" (helkyson).
notes.29:5: Greek hylodes lian ("exceedingly luxuriant," literally "very wooded") is a distinctive Septuagint reading where the Hebrew reads "when the Almighty was yet with me."
notes.29:7: Greek orthrios ("early in the morning") reflects reading the Hebrew word for "gate" as "dawn."
notes.29:18: Greek stelechos phoinikos ("trunk of a palm tree") renders Hebrew hol ("sand" or "phoenix") through Greek phoinix, which means both "palm tree" and "phoenix."
notes.29:20: The Greek text reads en cheiri autou ("in his hand"), contrasting with the Hebrew "in my hand"; ancient Greek interpreters sometimes understood this pronoun as referring to God's hand.
notes.30:4: Greek epi echounti ("by what resounds") and halima/alima ("saltwort" / "salt herbs") preserve the Septuagint's distinctive interpretation of the underlying Hebrew plant imagery.
notes.30:12: Greek epi dexion blastou ("at the right hand of the shoot") renders the Hebrew term for a rabble or brood with blastos ("shoot" or "sprout").
notes.30:24: The Septuagint distinctively expresses a wish to lay violent hands upon himself (emauton cheirosasthai) or ask another to do so, differing markedly from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.30:28: Greek aneu phimou ("without a muzzle") is a distinctive Septuagint reading where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "without the sun."
notes.31:2: This Greek text reads kai eti ("and moreover") as a declarative statement rather than a question; Hikanou (literally "of the Sufficient One") is the Septuagint's standard title for Shaddai ("the Almighty").
notes.31:23: Greek lemma ("burden" or "weight") denotes God's overwhelming charge or majesty, while phobos ("dread") stands without an explicit genitive "of God" in this Greek text.
notes.31:24: This Greek text reads eis choun mou ("as my dust," or "mound"), whereas some other Greek witnesses read eis ischyn mou ("as my strength").
notes.31:33: Greek akousios ("unwittingly" or "involuntarily") is the Septuagint reading where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "like Adam" (or "like men").
notes.31:35: In verses 35–37 the Septuagint frames Job's words around a written debt-bond (syngraphe) he held against a debtor (chreophiletou), which out of fear of the Lord he tore up and returned without taking payment.
notes.32:1: The Greek reads "before them" (in the sight of his three friends), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "in his own eyes."
notes.32:2: "Ausitis" is the Septuagint name for the land of Uz, added here in the Greek tradition to identify Elihu's region.
notes.32:7: The Septuagint reverses the sense of the Masoretic Hebrew here, having Elihu assert that time does not speak and many years do not know wisdom.
notes.32:17: The Greek introduces a narrative speech heading here ("Then Elihu answered and said"), whereas in the Masoretic Hebrew Elihu continues speaking in the first person.
notes.32:22: The Greek reads "moths also will eat me," diverging from the Masoretic Hebrew ("my Maker would soon take me away").
notes.33:14: The Greek syntax is elliptical, omitting the Hebrew clause "yet man does not perceive it" and linking "a second time" directly to the dream and nightly meditation in verse 15.
notes.33:23: The Septuagint reads "a thousand death-bearing angels" followed by a call to repentance, diverging markedly from the Masoretic Hebrew's "a mediator, one of a thousand."
notes.33:24: The Greek simile "like plaster upon a wall" for the renewal of the body is distinctive to the Septuagint tradition.
notes.33:30: The Greek shifts to the first person ("my soul ... my life") and reads "praise Him," differing from the third-person wording of the Masoretic Hebrew.
notes.34:6: In the Greek text, the verb is third-person singular ("He has dealt falsely with my judgment"), attributing the charge to the Lord, and "my arrow" (belos) preserves the Greek metaphor for an inflicted wound.
notes.34:8: The Septuagint uniquely includes "having not sinned nor acted ungodly," continuing Elihu's ironic rhetorical question about Job in contrast to the Masoretic Text.
notes.34:10: The Greek reads "Far be it from me to act ungodly before the Lord," expressing Elihu's own recoil from impiety, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Far be it from God to do wickedness."
notes.34:23: The Greek text of this verse is notably brief and elliptical compared with the longer Hebrew Masoretic Text, leaving the object of "lay" unexpressed.
notes.34:30: Unlike the Masoretic Text ("that a godless man should not reign"), the Septuagint states positively that God sets a hypocritical man as king because of the people's perversity.
notes.35:4: Verse 35:3 is absent from the Septuagint Greek text, and 35:4 specifically names Job's "three friends" where the Masoretic Text reads "your friends with you."
notes.35:10: The Greek reads "who appoints the night watches" (phylakas nykterinas) rather than the Masoretic Text's "who gives songs in the night."
notes.35:14: The Septuagint diverges markedly from the Masoretic Text here, stating that the Almighty beholds lawless deeds "and He shall save me," and challenging Job to be judged before Him "if you are able to praise Him as He is."
notes.36:14: The Greek reads "wounded by angels," a distinctive Septuagint rendering where the Hebrew Masoretic Text refers to ritual figures.
notes.36:28: Greek palaiomata ("ancient things," also in 37:18, 21) renders the Hebrew word for skies/clouds by etymological association with growing old; the second half of this verse is a Septuagint expansion absent from the Masoretic Text.
notes.36:30: The Greek reads "the song" (he ode), a distinctive Septuagint reading where the Hebrew text refers to His light or mist.
notes.36:33: The Greek clause is elliptical and reflects a different reading of the Hebrew consonants, yielding "His friend" and "a possession, even concerning unrighteousness."
notes.37:4: Greek hybreos literally means "pride" or "loftiness," used here in the Septuagint to express the overwhelming majesty of God's thunderous voice.
notes.37:12: The word "theebulathoth" is left untranslated in the Greek as a transliteration of the Hebrew noun tahbulot, meaning "guidance" or "steering."
notes.37:16: "The extraordinary downfalls of the wicked" is a distinctive Septuagint reading that diverges markedly from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.38:7: The Greek text reads "all My angels" rather than the Hebrew "all the sons of God," and speaks of the stars being made without specifying "morning stars."
notes.38:14: Rather than comparing the dawn-lit earth to clay under a seal as in the Masoretic Text, the Septuagint depicts the fashioning of a living creature endowed with speech from clay of the earth.
notes.38:30: The Greek reads "the face of the ungodly" (asebous) where the Hebrew text refers to "the face of the deep," reflecting a notable textual divergence preserved in the Septuagint.
notes.38:32: "Mazoroth" (Greek Mazourouth) transliterates a rare Hebrew astronomical term for a constellation or celestial cycle, paired here with "the Evening Star" (Hesperos).
notes.38:36: Where the Hebrew text speaks obscurely of wisdom in the inward parts or mind, the Septuagint renders the verse as a question about God granting women the wisdom of weaving and the skill of embroidery.
notes.39:7: The Septuagint renders the Hebrew "driver" as "tax collector" (phorologos), portraying the wild donkey as untouched by civic tribute and reproach.
notes.39:9: Greek monokeros literally denotes a "one-horned beast" (traditionally rendered "unicorn"), the standard Septuagint translation of the Hebrew re'em (wild ox).
notes.39:13: The Greek text leaves two Hebrew terms transliterated as "hasida" and "nessa" (in Hebrew referring to the stork and plumage), producing an elliptical clause rendered faithfully as it stands in Greek.
notes.39:20: Where the Hebrew text compares the warhorse to a leaping locust, the Septuagint describes him as outfitted in "full armor" (panoplia) with boldness adorning his breast.
notes.40:2: Greek Hikanos ("the Sufficient One") is the Septuagint's characteristic title rendering Hebrew Shaddai ("the Almighty") throughout Job.
notes.40:8: Unlike the Masoretic Text ("condemn Me that you may be justified"), the Greek asks whether God has dealt with Job for any other purpose than that he might be shown righteous.
notes.40:15: The Greek renders Hebrew Behemoth as the common plural noun theria ("wild beasts") with a plural verb, before shifting to singular pronouns in verse 16.
notes.40:19: Literally "made to be mocked by His angels," a distinctive Septuagint reading that recurs in 41:25.
notes.40:20: Greek tartaros ("Tartarus"), a cosmological term for the deepest abyss, is used here and again in 41:24.
notes.41:1: Verses 1 through 3 preserve a textual overlap characteristic of the Greek manuscript tradition, repeating the rhetorical questions "Do you not fear that he is prepared for Me?" and "For who is he who has withstood Me?"
notes.41:4: The Greek syntax is compressed, placing "a word of power" in the accusative as a complement of respect or cause before "he will pity his equal."
notes.41:22: Greek "gold of the sea" (chrysos thalasses) reflects a distinct reading of the Hebrew word for a sharp threshing sledge, which shares the same consonants as a poetic term for gold.
notes.41:24: Where the Masoretic Text pictures the deep as white-haired, the Greek portrays the dragon treating "the Tartarus of the abyss as a captive" and reckoning the abyss "as a walkway."
notes.42:3: The Greek differs markedly from the Hebrew, asking who hides counsel from God or spares words thinking to hide from Him, and asking who will declare the great and marvelous things Job did not know or understand.
notes.42:6: The Greek renders Job's confession as despising himself, melting away, and regarding himself as earth and ashes, rather than repenting in dust and ashes as in the Hebrew.
notes.42:9: The Greek identifies Zophar as "the Minaean" (Greek Meinaîos) rather than "the Naamathite" of the Hebrew text; similarly in 42:11 the friends' gifts appear as a ewe lamb and a tetradrachm of uncoined gold.
notes.42:14: The Greek renders the names of Job's daughters as Day, Cassia, and Horn of Amalthea (alluding to the Greek mythological horn of plenty), corresponding to Hebrew Jemimah, Keziah, and Keren-Happuch.
notes.42:17: Following the Greek lifespan figures in 42:16 (one hundred and seventy years after his affliction and two hundred and forty in total), this verse adds a Septuagint epilogue on Job's resurrection and genealogy from "the Syriac book" identifying him with Jobab in Ausitis (Uz), preserving Greek-distinct names such as Ennon, Balak (for Bela), Barad (for Bedad), and Geththaim (for Avith), and treating Bozrah as his mother's name.
